newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ wages data could quash Dec easing - economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ wages data could quash Dec easing - economists.

text.p: New Zealand wages data due Tuesday could quash for good the chances of a pre-Christmas easing in monetary policy, economists say.
And even if the August Quarterly Employment Survey comes in below consensus forecasts, that may not be enough to loosen the tourniquet this year.
"At the moment, you couldn't really put it at much more than a 50-50 chance," said BNZ Treasury Economist Peter Jolly.
Economists regard Tuesday's statistics, in particular the rise in private sector average hourly earnings, as crucial to the timing and extent of any easing.
"Wages make up around about 60 percent of inflation, the way the Reserve Bank looks at it, so it's obviously a very critical input," said Jolly.
In a Reuters survey, economists forecast a 3.5 percent rise in total average ordinary time earings and a 4.16 percent rise in private sector average hourly earnings for the year to August.

Jolly said an increase of 4.2 percent or less in the private sector, coming on top of weak retail sales data last week, would keep alive the chances of an easing in December. But he added: "A very strong rise, maybe towards the 4.5 percent region, would
pour a lot of cold water on that suggestion."

ANZ economist David Drage said it was important that Tuesday's data confirm wage inflation pressures had peaked in the June quarter, in keeping with the assumptions underpinning the Reserve Bank's inflation outlook.
But even then, the bank was likely to wait until it was sure inflationary pressures were starting to abate across the board before it signalled an easing.

"There's still some areas of ongoing concerns, particularly the housing market," said Drage. "What sort of response there's been to the recent mortgage rate cuts is still an area of quite considerable uncertainty."
He said the 3.2 percent rise in the Food Price Index in the year to October, particularly the 5.1 percent increase in grocery prices, was of "notable concern".
"There's some quite key things that will need to be seen before the Reserve Bank can feel comfortable -- probably most critically the December quarter CPI out in January," he said.
"Confirmation from that that the September quarter (CPI) number was on the nail could be the thing to provide the Reserve Bank with scope to allow conditions to ease significantly."
